title: Ancient Georgia Pottery Holds Earliest Chocolate Traces East of the Mississippi
summary:
Chocolate may have fueled the builders of ancient Georgia's earthen mounds. A new genetic study found traces of cacao — the plant that becomes chocolate — on pottery from Etowah, near Atlanta, dating to around the 11th century. It's the earliest known cacao east of the Mississippi River.

Cacao originated in Mesoamerica, where the Olmecs were making fermented chocolate drinks by 1500 B.C.E. The Maya even used cacao beans as currency. But Etowah is far from the tropical lowlands where cacao trees grow. How did the beans get there?

Archaeologists Adam King and Terry Powis analyzed residue on 31 pottery sherds from a feast held between 1050 and 1150 C.E. The feast remains were found in the 1950s in a borrow pit — a hole left after mining red clay for the mounds. The tallest mound once rose about 64 feet high. King and Powis found caffeine in all 31 sherds — but caffeine also comes from yaupon holly, a native plant. So they teamed up with French researchers to do DNA analysis. Two sherds contained cacao DNA. The DNA was degraded in a way consistent with being 1,000 years old, ruling out modern contamination.

"They take a lot of care to talk about why they don't think it's modern contamination," says archaeologist Barbara Mills, who wasn't involved in the study. "I thought they did a really great job."

The discovery suggests vast trade networks connected the ancient Americas. Cacao may have traveled from Chaco Canyon in New Mexico, along the Gulf Coast, or through the Caribbean. "There are continental scale trade networks," Mills says.

The Muscogee people, who hold Etowah sacred, gave permission for the analysis. The mounds themselves may have symbolized the Earth — building them was like re-enacting creation. Finishing a mound likely called for a feast. Now we know chocolate may have been on the menu.
why_it_matters: For anyone studying history, this is evidence that ancient North America was not a patchwork of isolated villages but a continent linked by long-distance trade — and it shows how new genetic tools, used with the permission of Indigenous nations, keep rewriting what we thought we knew.

background_read: Etowah (an ancient Native American mound site in Georgia, near Atlanta) was built by ancestors of the Muscogee people, who still hold the site sacred and had to give permission before the pottery was tested. Cacao — the plant whose seeds become chocolate — was first domesticated in Mesoamerica (a region covering southern Mexico and much of Central America). There the Olmecs (an early civilization that flourished more than 3,000 years ago) were brewing fermented chocolate drinks by 1500 B.C.E., and the Maya (a later Mesoamerican civilization known for its cities and writing) valued cacao beans so highly that they used them as money. In Mesoamerica chocolate was a bitter, spiced drink, not a sweet bar.

Mesoamerican cacao has turned up far from the tropics before: traces were found in jars at Chaco Canyon (a huge ancestral Puebloan centre in New Mexico, occupied roughly a thousand years ago), which suggests beans travelled north along long-distance trade routes. The Mississippian peoples of the southeastern United States built earthen mounds as platforms for temples, tombs and leaders' houses, and finishing a mound was often marked with a big feast. Archaeologists test residues inside old pottery because the pots themselves are often plain, and soft remains like cacao almost never survive in humid southeastern soil.

perspectives.description: The study adds hard evidence that cacao, a tropical luxury, reached Georgia a thousand years ago, and it was done only after the Muscogee people, who hold Etowah sacred, gave permission — a model many researchers now see as the right way to work at such sites.
The proof rests on DNA from just two sherds, and ancient DNA is notoriously easy to contaminate; critics would want many more samples from more sites before treating the trade route as settled.

Seen over the long run, chocolate keeps appearing far from where it grows: cacao residues at Chaco Canyon and now at Etowah fit a wider pattern of exchange linking Mesoamerica, the American Southwest and the Southeast.
More residue testing at other mound sites could map the route the beans travelled, and further work may show whether cacao was drunk as a bitter beverage at feasts or used in some other way entirely.
